check_iss_over_area.description: Check whether the space station is over an area you mark out with four edges of latitude and longitude, such as a box around a country or a stretch of ocean, so a scheduled workflow can post when it is overhead. Open Notify reports only the point below the station, so the comparison is done here, and an area whose western edge is east of its eastern edge wraps across the 180th meridian, so the middle of the Pacific can be one area. The point checked is where Open Notify puts the station, which in November 2026 was about 7,600 km from where it really was. No API key required.

check_iss_visibility.description: Check whether the space station could be seen with the naked eye from a place right now: high enough above the horizon there, still lit by the sun, and against a sky dark enough for it to stand out. Each of the three is returned on its own, with a sentence saying why when the answer is no, so a scheduled workflow can send an alert only when it is worth going outside. Open Notify reports only where the station is, so all of this is worked out from that position, the time and where the sun is. It does not know about cloud, and it answers for this moment, not when the station will next pass. The position itself has drifted: in November 2026 Open Notify put the station about 7,600 km from where it really was. No API key required.

This is the one action that reports a problem as a value instead of failing the step, so a workflow can decide what to do about it. Being asked to slow down is reported separately from being down. get_distance_to_iss.description: Answer 'is the space station near me?' for a place on the ground: how far away it is in kilometres and miles, which compass direction to look in, and whether it is above the horizon there at all. Open Notify reports only where the station is, never how that relates to anywhere, so the comparison is done here. The distance is from where Open Notify puts the station, which in November 2026 was about 7,600 km from where it really was. No API key required.

get_iss_position.description: Get where the International Space Station is right now: the latitude and longitude of the point on the ground directly below it, the instant that position is for, and a map link to open it. The station covers about 28,000 km every hour, so the answer is only good for a few seconds. Open Notify works the position out from orbit data that has fallen behind, so it can be thousands of kilometres from where the station really is: about 7,600 km in November 2026. Use Where the ISS At? when the position has to be right. No API key required.

get_people_in_space.description: Get who Open Notify lists as being in space, with the spacecraft each person is aboard and a count per craft, so a step can say how many are on the station without counting a list itself. Name a spacecraft to get only its crew. Nobody aboard is an empty result rather than a failed step. The service's maintainer keeps the list by hand, and it can be months behind real launches and landings, so treat it as the service's list rather than an official record. No API key required.

sample_iss_track.description: Watch the station move: take several positions a few seconds apart and get the path between them, how far it travelled, how fast and which way it is heading. Open Notify only ever reports where the station is at the present instant, so this step waits between readings at the cadence the service asks for, which is why it takes as long as it does, and works the distance, speed and heading out from them. No API key required.
sample_iss_track.name: sample_iss_track

parameters.description: How many readings to take, from 2 to 10. Each one after the first waits out the gap below, so the step takes roughly that gap times one less than this.
parameters.name: count

parameters.description: How long to wait between readings, from 5 to 60 seconds. Open Notify works the position out once a second and asks callers to poll about once every five, so anything shorter is refused.
parameters.name: interval_seconds

parameters.description: The height above the ground to assume for the station, in kilometres. Open Notify reports no altitude, so the figures derived from one assume 420 km, the station's usual operating height. Change it to match a published altitude if you have one.
parameters.name: altitude_km

assumed_altitude_km.description: The altitude the orbital speed was worked out from. Open Notify publishes none.

elapsed_seconds.description: Seconds between the first and last reading, by the service's own timestamps, which are whole seconds.

end_time.description: When the last reading was for.

ground_distance_km.description: How far the point below the station moved across the Earth over that span.

ground_speed_kmh.description: That distance as a speed, in kilometres per hour: how fast the station's shadow crosses the ground, about 24,850 km/h. Over a single five-second gap it can be a tenth out either way, because Open Notify's positions move in half-second steps; more readings narrow that.

heading_compass_point.description: The same heading as a compass point, e.g. 'NE'.

heading_degrees.description: Which way the station was moving over the last two readings, in degrees clockwise from north. Worked out from the readings, since Open Notify reports no heading; empty if they were the same point.

interval_seconds.description: The gap asked for between readings.

measured_seconds.description: The same span timed from when each answer arrived, kept within a second of the service's timestamps. The speeds are worked out over this. Open Notify's positions move in half-second steps, so it can still be half a second out at each end. Empty if the service sent no timestamps.

orbital_speed_kmh.description: How fast the station itself is travelling, which is faster than its shadow because it sweeps a wider circle and the ground below it turns with the Earth. Worked out from the readings with the Earth's turn taken out and from the assumed altitude, so it is an estimate: about 27,600 km/h, and as far out as the ground speed over a short track.

latitude.description: Latitude of the point on the ground directly below the station, in degrees. Negative is south of the equator. The service quotes this as a string; it is published here as a number.

longitude.description: Longitude of that point, in degrees. Negative is west of the Greenwich meridian.

map_url.description: Map link centred on the point below the station.

time.description: The same instant as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time.

timestamp.description: The instant this position is for, in Unix seconds.

start_time.description: When the first reading was for, as an ISO 8601 UTC date-time.

description: Track the International Space Station with Open Notify, the free keyless API behind open-notify.org. Get where the station is right now and who the service lists in space, how far away the station is from any place on Earth, whether it could be seen from there right now, whether it is over an area you mark out, or watch it move across several readings to see how fast and which way it is going. Open Notify's position has drifted from the station's real one, by about 7,600 km in November 2026, so use Where the ISS At? when it has to be right. There is one action that reports the service's own health as a value rather than failing a step, so a scheduled workflow can tell an outage from an empty answer. No account and no API key: connecting takes one click.
